speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-53, an act to amend the Criminal Code (arson), as reported (with an amendment) from a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is one motion on the notice paper offered in amendment to the report stage of Bill C-53, an act to amend the Criminal Code (arson), standing in the name of the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River.

The House will now proceed with motion numbered 1. [English]

That Bill C-53 be amended in Clause 1 by striking out lines 26 to 45 at page 2 and substituting the following therefor:
"436. Every person who owns, in whole or in part, or controls property is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years where
(a)	that person wilfully or recklessly disregards the life or safety of another person or the security of property by failing to comply with any law respecting the prevention of fires or explosions in the property; and
(b)	the failure to comply with a law mentioned in paragraph (a) is a cause of a fire or an explosion in the property which causes bodily harm to another person or damage to property."
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise at this time to speak to my amendment to Bill C-53, a bill providing for reform of the arson legislation.
Section 436 as it is proposed now in the government's Bill C-53 purports to create a new offence which has been generally called "arson by negligence" where fire results from a degree of negligence. The key words and thrust of the new section are that a person would be guilty of an offence under that section if the person is a cause of a fire-and that does not mean the cause but a cause, among others-and where the fire is the result of a marked departure from a standard of care that a reasonably prudent person would use.
The issue that that raises is this. What is a marked departure from that standard of care? Here we are forced to use some hypotheticals. It could be a careless or a stupid act like leaving an open can of gasoline next to a furnace burner in a basement, or it could simply be an omission.
Here I would use a hypothetical something like a senior citizen of advanced years living in his or her home who fails to correct substandard wiring in their home. That is assuming that the wiring as it exists now does not comply with existing municipal by-law standards.
The proposed Section 436 does not leave us without any help as to what a marked departure from that standard is.
Subsection (2) of the proposed section permits a court to infer a marked departure from a standard of care where there is a failure to comply with any law respecting the prevention of fires. In this case of a by-law governing an electrical wiring, I think I could reasonably infer that that was the purpose of such a by-law.
In this particular hypothetical we have a situation where this person, perhaps of advanced years, and perhaps not as mindful of things as he or she might have been in their youth, fails to comply with the municipal by-law, whether or not they knew it, because the section does not require the person who breaches the municipal by-law to know that they breached it. Nor does it require

May 4, 1990
Government Orders
a conviction. Whether or not they knew they were in breach of the by-law, it permits a court to infer that there was a marked departure.
In that hypothetical we have created a situation where a person has become criminally liable, someone who did not intend to become criminally liable and who did not know that they were criminally liable.
In our criminal law we have certain safeguards which have been with us for years-almost for centuries, I could say. We go back to the Magna Carta for that purpose.
To be guilty of a criminal act, there must be an act or an omission of some sort, and there must be an element accompanying that which manifests an intention to do the act or to fail to act, in the case of an omission.
However, in this case we have a person who, in my view, never had the intention to be a criminal and did not know an offence was committed until afterward when the Crown Attorney becomes the lightning rod for all the anger and frustration that usually accompanies a tragic fire of this sort.
That is not how our criminal law is supposed to work. How can we deter citizens from committing offences if they do not know they are committing them as they go about their lives? In this case the person really would not know they had been guilty of an offence until afterward when a charge was laid and they were convicted.
There are three problems that have been cited in connection with this section dealing with arson by negligence. The first is that it creates a fuzzy standard, one that has not been used before. The standard of a marked departure from a standard of care that a reasonably prudent person would use is a standard that is used in the civil law, but not the criminal law.
Second, the section purports to impose what lawyers and law professors call an "objective standard" relative to the mental element or intention of the criminal offence I referred to earlier. The Supreme Court has divided on a couple of occasions on the issue of whether it will permit the criminal law to use an objective standard. There is a continuing sense that we must have
a subjective standard, a subjective reference point when dealing with the intention of an alleged criminal.
Third, there is some consensus in some quarters that this provision as it is may bump up against and fail because of the Section 7 guarantees of fundamental justice in our Charter.
What this section really does is permit a Crown attorney to say to the court: "Your Honour, here are the facts. Here is the tragic result. You decide whether this person was a good guy or a bad guy, and if you want to convict him, go ahead". Meanwhile, this good guy or bad guy never knew that he or she was a good guy or a bad guy in the hypothetical I presented, and that is not right.
The amendment I propose targets those who advertently, wilfully and recklessly endanger life or safety by failing to comply with any law with respect to the prevention of fires or explosions.
The concept of criminal negligence which I would use is already incorporated in our Criminal Code. The provisions of wilfulness, recklessness and disregard for life are elements that deal with the intention or mental element I referred to earlier. The section is viable under the Charter. It has been tested and we currently use it, for example, in criminal negligence cases causing loss of life and in motor vehicle cases involving negligence.
If we pass the government's proposed Section 436, we leave open the possibility of a court challenge. The Department of Justice knows that it is breaking new ground with this section, new ground that presents risks to our civil liberties vis-a-vis the protections we have in our criminal law. If this section does not survive a court challenge, then we have succeeded in creating a new section of the Criminal Code that is just as clumsy and unworkable as those old outmoded clumsy sections we have been trying to replace through reform. That is the risk which I submit the government is taking at this time.
The Canadian Bar Association supports this amendment. In fact, it has drafted it. I will not take credit for its drafting. I am pleased to present this amendment to the House.
May 4, 1990

I challenge the government not to gamble with these uncertain standards and not to permit a court challenge dealing with validity involving the Criminal Code standards or Section 7 of the Charter.
I urge the government not to permit the Department of Justice to continue to live life in the fast lane like this and to support my amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on this bill to amend the arson legislation. These measures will, as we know, result in tougher criminal sanctions for arson, particularly in cases resulting in bodily harm or in arson involving homes or other residences. Those tougher criminal sanctions are to be welcomed.
It is to be noted, too, that this is the first major change to the Criminal Code provisions on arson in this century since 1892. We are dealing with an area which we have not rushed into in the past, but it is an important area to which we should pay careful attention.
With regard to Section 436 and the amendment proposed by the member for Scarborough-Rouge River, we have some major concerns with the terminology used in the government's version of the section to which the hon. member has referred.
He quite rightly pointed out that a person could be charged with a criminal offence for not being the cause of a fire but for being a cause of a fire. It is not that I have so many concerns about that if one or a number of people are engaged in ensuring that arson takes place. The more important concern is with regard to the standard or to the test which will be applied as to whether or not a person will be found guilty of the offence.
At best, it is a nebulous charge. It may be, as has been pointed out, that it will be rendered unconstitutional.
I would like to read the proposed terminology in the government's bill. It states that a person would be liable "where, as a result of a marked departure from the standard of care that a reasonably prudent person would use to prevent fires or explosions, that person is a cause of a fire or explosion in that property that causes bodily harm to another person or damage to property".
Government Orders
We would, of course, always have some concerns and some uncertainties as to what is meant by a marked departure, although some statements by the Supreme Court of Canada certainly suggest that that is a reasonable guideline. I will come back to that.
There is clearly some uncertainty about what will be meant by "a marked departure". That would leave Canadians uncertain as to the behaviour expected of them, leading up to any potential criminal offence. Indeed, leading up to and after a case of arson, they would not know, nor would they be able to know, what standard of care was expected of them, what would be a marked departure from that standard of care and what would not be.
We also have difficult problems of predictability when we use a standard of care that is expected of a reasonably prudent person. It is, as has been pointed out, the standard used in assessing civil actions, for instance, whether or not in a motor vehicle accident somebody has acted in a way which would not meet the standard of care expected of a reasonably prudent driver of a motor vehicle.
We have not explored the opportunities for using those sorts of standards in the Criminal Code. I think it unwise to suggest to Canadians that they will be treated as criminals and, indeed, will be punished as criminals when the activity that they pursue is not deliberate activity but is activity which is negligent, and not of any particular level of negligence either. In the terminology of "marked departure" there is some lesser degree of negligence than, for example, there is with gross negligence.
It is not generally expected by Canadians that they will be treated as criminals unless they have the intention to be criminals. There are some exceptions, but I think in the case of arson, and in this case, we do not need to go as far as to make negligent Canadians criminals in this regard. That is not to say that we should not be tightening the rules with regard to arson. As I said, my party and I welcome that.
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River is to make the provisions clearly more certain for those who might be involved, and also to ensure that those who are treated as criminals are people who have done something deliberately or sufficiently recklessly as to almost make it deliberate in the activity involved.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill, Bill C-53, has received wide support.
The only provision on which there is a difference of opinion is that contained in the definition of negligent arson. The government accepted the suggestion made by the Canadian Bar Association concerning the area covered by this offence.

However, there still remains a difference of opinion as to which definition of negligence should be adopted.
The hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River in his Notice of Motion has advanced the definition proposed by the Canadian Bar Association. The government, having been urged by a number of persons to retain an offence of arson by negligence, in this bill has favoured the test for negligence proposed by the Law Reform Commission of Canada in its report 31.
Although, in most cases the two tests would produce the same result, they would lead to a different result where, on the evidence, it is clear that a property owner or manager neglected to maintain his or her property and the neglect was a cause of a fire or explosion in that property which caused bodily harm to another or damaged a property.
Under the formulation of the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River, the issue before the court would be whether the owner or manager had been reckless in that he or she had been aware of the risk of fire or explosions. Such an owner could argue that he or she was never consciously aware of a risk of fire, but just neglected the premises. In effect, the owner would be permitted to turn a blind eye to the risk of fire, and if believed would be acquitted.
I could go further and say that the amendment as proposed by the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River requires, as a preliminary threshold for establishing an offence under this section, that a person has failed to comply with any law because wilful or reckless regard for the life or safety of another person is defined as failing to comply with any law respecting the prevention of fires or explosions in the property. There is an initial threshold that has to be overcome to establish that there
May 4, 1990

is a law in place, whether that would be a provincial law or a municipal bylaw, that that law has been breached by the person in question and then criminal liability results from that.
I believe the formulation which the government favours is one that is a little broader and which takes into account the inherent nature of the behaviour of the person who is accused irrespective of whether that behaviour can be found to come within an existing legal framework; in other words, whether a law has been breached. The preliminary threshold of establishing the existence of a law and its breach prior to establishing the mens rea sufficient to convict under this section is not a barrier which is in the government's formulation.
I think it is very important because the whole notion of the law of negligence is that there are obligations and duties in society that may not be statutory but that are nonetheless obligations and duties that individuals can be bound by in their responsibility to their fellow man, and that is the duty of care as we discuss in the law of negligence.
Under the government's formulation, the issue before the court would be whether the accused's conduct constituted a marked departure from the standard of care that a reasonably prudent person would use. Under the government's formulation, the property owner or manager would not be allowed to turn a blind eye to the deterioration of the premises as a result of his or her neglect and would be convicted irrespective of whether a law relating to the premises had been breached.
As between the two tests, the government's formulation would place an unmistakable onus on those who own or operate multiple-unit dwellings, especially rooming houses, to not neglect their properties to the point that they become fire traps.
We have chosen to proceed with the government's formulation because we have an obligation to do all the law can to ensure the safety of those who live in these units, many of whom have no other place to go.
With respect to the comments of my colleague from Scarborough-Rouge River and further to what was indicated by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Clark's
Government Orders
Crossing, on the terminology "marked departure", that test was taken from the judgment of Mr. Justice McIntyre, as he then was in the Supreme Court of Canada in its decision in the Tutton case. The marked departure will be a question of fact in every case. In the scenario described by my colleague from Scarborough-Rouge River, I believe marked departure is a high threshold which has to be established before liability can attach. The examples the hon. member used would not likely constitute marked departure.
I would argue that the government's formulation which is taken from the recommendation of the Law Reform Commission is better in that it reduces the two-stage threshold; the need to establish the existence of a law that has not been complied with before criminal liability can be found under this act, that criminal liability relates directly to the actual behaviour of the person who is accused and whether that behaviour is a marked departure from the standard of care that a reasonably prudent person would be found to be obliged to observe.
On that basis, I wish to indicate my support for the government's formulation of this clause in the bill. I intend to speak against the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, we are debating an act to reconstitute the courts in British Columbia.
This bill is not a controversial piece of legislation, but it is important to recognize that the business of the House does not work very effectively if members are not able to present their positions on bills like this. On the bill that was of some importance today, the bill dealing with arson, there were members who wanted to speak, but unfortunately they were not given the opportunity to do so. Two speakers stood but they were not recognized, and consequently things happened then which nobody particularly wanted to happen.
We are now dealing with legislation to merge the county courts in British Columbia with the Supreme Court, a move which has been taking place across the country. The opportunity is for courts to be more as one court, rather than a range of courts, still under the jurisdiction of the federal government.
The provinces are supportive of the measure, and it certainly seems desired by the province of British Columbia. Once we have dealt with Ontario, this would leave only the Nova Scotia court system with a divided trial court jurisdiction.
We are seeing movements across the country to bring federal courts together under one aegis, if you like. We have supported this merger and will continue to support it. It should result in a more effective court system across
Government Orders
British Columbia and the other provinces where it has been adopted.
There are some matters with judges and the courts which we might want to refer to in dealing with this piece of legislation. We have, over the last while, seen comments made by judges on a range of activities which should give concern to the federal government. One matter in particular is giving concern to the members in the New Democratic Party, and that is the independence of the judiciary.
There is a case in Quebec of a family court judge speaking out against inadequate services for the protection of children. She now finds herself being accused of improper conduct for not following the normal procedures expected of judges. Surely, we do not expect our judges to close their minds to the things going on around them. We should expect them to take a leadership role in pointing out matters which they feel concerning our society, and in particular, those which they encounter as a result of the activities they pursue on a regular basis. If they do recognize that services are inadequate and they cannot do their job effectively because of, for example, inadequate social services, then it is important that they be able to speak out against them.
I think it is important for all of us to recognize and support judges who do speak out against injustices in our society. We know of other judges faced with that problem. A former leader in British Columbia, Mr. Justice Berger, was faced with some of those concerns as well. He felt that he was unable to speak out on important constitutional matters and found it no longer possible to stay on the bench as a result of those restrictions.
While discussing the proposals to put county courts and the Supreme Court of British Columbia under one organization, it is important to recognize that not all is well with the way in which our judges are treated and the way in which we, as a society, can make use of judges both on and off the bench.
We have concerns, as we have all heard, over the recent while of male judges in particular, not speaking in favourable terms towards women and indeed being insulting toward women from the bench. We know that that does not help the public view the courts with the appropriate level of respect that is needed in the circumstances.

We have concerns about the way in which the courts operate. We think it is important that the courts be streamlined so they will become more efficient and effective. We have to bear in mind that not everything that judges do is well regarded, especially when they attack and insult Canadians. We hope these concerns will be treated in the appropriate way. It is important that judges who do make attacks on women that have been the victims of various sorts of abuse, are chastised and not permitted to carry on in the way in which they have done in the past. It is important for all of us to speak out against that.
The NDP is in favour of this bill, and we are supporting the merger of the courts in British Columbia, the county courts with the Supreme Court.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-59. I hope we have an opportunity to hear from the Minister of Justice on a couple of points that I am going to raise.
The concept of the merging of courts is something that has been going on for a long period of time, not just in Canada and British Columbia but in many areas of the world. This is in part because of the duplication of some services and the more appropriate delivery of services that one gets with a more streamlined system.
British Columbia is a case in point where we have the former Chief Justice of the British Columbia Supreme Court, now the Chief Justice of the British Columbia Court of Appeal, Mr. McEachern. At this time, rather than being seized with mostly Court of Appeal actions, Mr. Justice McEachern is seized with one of the most important matters ever to come before the Supreme Court of British Columbia, that is the Gitksan-Wet'Su-wet'en trial that is presently in its final stages in Smithers, in northwestern British Columbia.
After many years of having worked in all levels of the courts in British Columbia as an officer of the court, in many cases that might go to the Supreme Court or to the Court of Appeal, they will be better dealt with by having, what might be described as the umbrella approach in relation to cases that are on appeal. Also, this happens where various kinds of injunctive actions are being sought, such as those that have been sought in relation to many First Nations cases and so on.
We on this side would like to hear from the Minister of Justice about that part of the bill which deals with money matters, and clause 25 is obviously the part that relates to salaries of judges. One of the great problems being faced in British Columbia is having access to funds to take various matters to the court, which is something that has been raised many times in this House.
This is not only in relation to charter and constitutional matters, but to one of the most serious problems that we have in British Columbia at the moment. It is one that is continuing to accelerate on both the legal and political scale, and that is in relation to matters facing First Nations. Since the Minister of Justice has chosen to use this B.C. court amendment to deal with money matters, we on this side, following Question Period, very much look forward to hearing from the minister.
We want to know why, if some money matters were chosen to be dealt with in relation to salaries, the same kind of opportunity was not chosen to introduce into the bill, a somewhat more compassionate and realistic reflection of the needs in British Columbia for access. They need access until this bill is passed by Governor in Council, for matters that either end up in the Supreme Court of British Columbia, such as the Gitksan-Wet'Su-wet'en trial and others, or matters that end up at the B.C. Court of Appeal.
There are matters such as the Meares Island case and others, where there are groups whose rights are being abridged and violated. In a province like British Columbia there is a great need for access to funds. They need it not just for legal counsel but also to prepare cases that are becoming increasingly complex. In relation to recent rulings of the Supreme Court of Canada, we know of the need for small groups to have access to funds to protect their rights.
In a province like British Columbia, access to funds is needed so aboriginal peoples, in particular, can properly prepare themselves in relation to historic treaties and in relations with the provincial or federal legislatures. I look forward to hearing the Minister of Justice who, perhaps has plans to attach to this other financial proposals, of which I think funding access to the courts would be the most important.

Mr. Speaker, the goods and services tax, Canada's answer to the European Community's value added tax, is an excellent target for the opposition to hone its expertise for scaring and misinforming Canadians, a talent they developed during the last election.
People are worried, but they are slowly becoming angry. They are no longer satisfied with the hollow opposition rhetoric and are demanding information. In my office, we have responded to hundreds and hundreds of requests for information about the goods and services tax.
I have received outright support and qualified acceptance for the GST and, of course, some people remain to be convinced. I am sure time will show Canadians that this tough political decision will create a fairer tax system and a stronger country. The Liberal members of the other place know this, which is why they have already begun to stall passage of the bill. There is more concern for the welfare of the Liberal party in the other place than there is for the welfare of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, after two years of gradually losing his patience, the commissioner of Official Languages has repeated his threat to resign because of the government's failure to table its draft regulations arising from the Official Languages Act.
The Federation des francophones hors Quebec, the national organization which represents francophone minorities in Canada, has now withdrawn from consultations with Treasury Board.
Mr. Speaker, the FFHQ refuses to be a party to this government's manoeuvring to delay indefinitely the implementation of the Official Languages Act. The government's reluctance to implement a policy it has been bragging about for two years is both incomprehensible and unacceptable. The time for consultation is over. Language minorities want action. If the Prime Minister is at all serious about this matter, he will accept my invitation to appear before the committee on Official Languages and explain his government's inability to table in the House the regulations arising from this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, there is increased concern over the growth in drug trafficking in Canada and the laundering of illegal drug money into the global financial system.
Today, I want to commend Donald Fullerton, the head of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce for his "get tough" recommendation. Mr. Fullerton said: "Banks that knowingly launder money by electronic transactions should be barred from the system that makes those transactions possible".
Money laundering involves about $85 billion U.S. a year in Europe and North America, according to a task force report. "We need to put teeth into the codes of conduct governing our members", said Mr. Fullerton, "and we need the courage to be ruthless with those who break the rules".
I call upon this government to initiate the brutal action required.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are well aware of the Prime Minister's fetish for Guccis and Perrier. Today, we read in La Presse newspaper that two food tasters accompanied him on his recent trip to the Atlantic provinces. This raises many interesting questions.

May 4, 1990
Are these the first food tasters to travel with him? If not, what happened to the previous ones? Have these jobs been given a high risk factor, given that the PM has broken all records for unpopularity?
We also read that the Tories are having a special caucus meeting this weekend. Rumours persist that two former caucus members from Alberta were recently spied in the cookbook section of Coles bookstore and could be masquerading as chefs at Mont Tremblant this weekend.
I would suggest to the PM that, in the event that the GST is on his political menu, perhaps he should pass on the beef cordon bleu and pears flambe this weekend, and opt instead for brown bag "baloney" sandwiches, a meat delicacy we know he must love because Canadians are constantly telling us he is full of it.

Mr. Speaker, VIA Rail's 1989 annual report is out and it reveals a very different picture from that given by the Conservatives.
The Tories claimed that Canadians were giving up on the trains. In fact, ridership was up and trains were more full. The Tories claimed the revenue was down and costs were up. In fact, VIA was costing less and making more. The first six months of 1989 showed a 4 per cent increase over the same period of 1988. It was only after a 10 per cent fare increase was forced on VIA by the Conservatives that the corporation's progress faltered. The crippling of VIA by the Conservatives through arbitrary cuts, uncertainty and privatization of popular routes such as the Rocky Mountaineer reveal a group of politicians determined to destroy a transportation service popular and needed among Canadians.
More cuts are now proposed and the target is the remote lines which VIA operates as a mandatory part of the network. To those who understand the environmental and the economic value of passenger trains in Canada, these cuts reveal Conservative policy as dangerously ignorant and biased against the west, biased against rural Canada, and biased against common sense.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister yesterday brought good news to Atlantic Canada by announcing that the data processing centre that will administer the goods and services tax will be established in Summerside, Prince Edward Island.
This new centre will create 400 direct full and parttime jobs for the people of Summerside, in addition to 100 indirect jobs and is further evidence of this government's commitment to generate economic growth in the regions of the country.
As Premier Ghiz so aptly stated: "This announcement is a fulfilment of the Prime Minister's personal leadership and a symbol of the kind of reconciliation and fairness that Canadian federalism is all about. I applaud the Prime Minister's initiative on behalf of the people of Summerside and look forward to more good news for Atlantic Canada".

Mr. Speaker, the current government has systematically brought Canadian businessmen to their knees with its unrelenting policy of high interest rates. With the bank prime set in excess of 14.25 per cent, which means that many businesses pay 1 to 2 per cent higher than that, small businesses are now on the brink of financial disaster.
As well, it is throwing all of the government's claims of deficit reduction and on-track budgeting of federal finances out of reach. A 1 per cent increase in the central bank's interest rate hikes the deficit by $1.7 billion. How can their claims to being fiscally responsible be considered as credible? More appropriately, I would call those claims by the government incredible.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to tree and forest week, from May 6 to May 12. This year's theme is: Our forests as a resource. The purpose of this theme is

Canadians are now witnessing the obvious signs of a threatened economy. Interest rates are at their highest level in eight years, bankruptcies are 30 per cent higher than they were at this time last year, and for the first time since the recession in 1982, our gross domestic product has dropped for two months in a row.

Mr. Speaker, multiple sclerosis is the most common disease of the central nervous system which usually strikes young adults in the prime of their life.
To call attention to this disease and those who must live with it, the month of May has been designated multiple sclerosis month by the Multiple Sclerosis Society of Canada. Mr. Speaker, once again the ruthlessness of this government has been revealed for all to see.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN AND CANADIAN CONTROL OF MINES EXTRACTING INDUSTRIAL METALS IN CANADA
speechtext:
Is the government aware of the percentage of (a) foreign ownership (b) Canadian ownership of mines extracting industrial metals (other than gold) in Canada, from 1975 to 1987 and, if so, what is it?
The data show a continuing decrease in foreign control for industrial metals during the period 1975 to 1986; the level of foreign participation dropped by 28 per cent. The concomitant increase in Canadian control is particularly evident between 1979 and 1985 as the degree of Canadian participation increased by 25 per cent.
In determining the level of foreign/Canadian participation in a sector, Statistics Canada does not measure ownership per se, but instead measures control. This is done by identifying the country of residence of the shareholder(s) exercising effective control over each company included in the sample. Companies are included in the sample if their annual revenues exceed $15 million. In measuring control levels within a sector, individual companies are weighed according to then-annual revenues. For more details on methodology, please refer to Statistics Canada's Annual Report pursuant to the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, Part I-Corporations.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-60 is similar in concept to Bill C-59 which governed the B.C. courts. I did not speak on behalf of my party in connection with Bill C-59 and deferred my remarks to Bill C-60.
Although it is technical in nature, this federal statute governing the Ontario courts like the B.C. courts permits unification of the courts at the Supreme Court level in the province and at the District Court level. In our view, it is fair to say that these courts are now finally
May 4, 1990

entering the 20th century-just in time; we have another 10 years to go.
Previously our provincial courts were divided into separate jurisdictions, usually based on monetary jurisdiction, with disputes involving larger dollar amounts being decided by the Superior Court and with lower dollar amounts being decided by the County or District Courts. It is a little bit like being a referee in the NHL and being a referee in the AHL. You are dealing with the same rules of the hockey game, but you have a slightly different environment and different players. I recall, as a lawyer, having to gown for one court but not for another. It was a little artificial.
The concept was based on life as it was in the last century. It has become counterproductive and inefficient. We have two sets of courts, two sets of judges, two sets of staff and two sets of courtrooms. With a united court in our provinces, we will be better able to manage and maximize the resources that we have in the court system on behalf of the taxpayers.
Although it is very easy for us at the federal level to pass this statute, we could not fail to acknowledge the work of many judges, court administrators and lawyers in the court systems in Ontario and in British Columbia in bringing these reforms into being. This will definitely benefit the taxpayer and improve the administration of justice. My party supports this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am particularly delighted to speak to the third reading of this bill. I hope it has quick passage through this House.
I would like to look at the process, something that is extremely exciting and dynamic. It comes at a particularly important time in the history of this House. If one looks at it in terms of time, this is Volunteer Week, or just a couple of days after.
This kirid of bill demonstrates in the most forceful, practical and important ways the role that volunteers play in society. When there is a group of like-minded people-in this instance, women-who have a serious concern about what an inequality or a gender biased situation within the laws of Canada, it prevents the forward movement of women to make enlightened choices and then to move forward with their lives.
I recall that in 1984-85 and early in 1986-1 see a nod from a brand new colleague from across the floor, along with my colleagues from York Centre and Burnaby. In particular, I remember the member for Saint John-that we sat and pondered what to do about this new dilemma, the Jewish get, as we were in the process of amending the divorce bill. It required a new look, and certainly an update. I was particularly appreciative of the sensitivity shown by the Minister of Justice of the day, followed by the new Minister of Justice of the day at that time, who is now the Governor General of this country, and followed by the third Minister of Justice of the day, who is now the Minister of Transport, and now we have our first woman in this very important role. You can see how key it was from 1985-86 to today, to have understanding on the part of all members of the House, as they looked at the application of fairness, justice and equality, under the law.
As a member of the small task force, section 15, on equality for all, I can remember even looking at it as far back as that time, in the history of my place in this House. The measure means a very great deal to me as a

May 4, 1990
Government Orders
Jewish woman, to the Jewish community and, in particular to those who have had to have a sense of discomfort, discrimination and bias, and also that very unpleasant sense that you are placed in a position of extortion in order to receive what is your due and what is your right under Canadian law. That is the key, it is under Canadian law. We are facilitating a divorce procedure which, in the Jewish traditional law, can only be undertaken as an act between the man and woman themselves in the presence of a rabbinical court of three members.
In a sense this traditional Jewish law, this Halachahic law, allowed for goodwill and the exchange of a document between a man and a woman, a man offers and the woman accepts this document. Where there was malicious intent or wilful desire to make life very difficult and to use this as a means of getting ends other than the right to proceed with one's life either as a man or a woman, more often than not it was a woman, this instrument or document was used in a manner that was not foreseen and there was no rabbinical court to which this could be taken.
I would like to say that in the interest of these women who got together, and in the interest of Volunteer Week, they forced an enlightened view to bring about the passage of a bill eliminating the unfairness which sometimes prevents Jewish persons from remarrying within their faith. We now have, thanks to the coalition of Jewish women for the get, Norma Joseph who was their driving force and John Surtash who was legal counsel, the first steps in the province of Ontario. I would like to bring to the attention of the minister, although she may may be well aware of it, that passage of this bill which is a landmark act internationally, never mind nationally, will certainly be used effectively by the women volunteers and the rabbis. In the province of Quebec rabbis found some very creative ways to enable this Jewish get or Jewish divorce, the rabbinical kind of approach which was outside of the civil process, to take place. They will use this bill to enable other governments in other countries to bring about justice for women in our society. In that light, as well, I want to express the very deepest appreciation of all of us, and particularly Jewish women, at this time.
On behalf of the Liberal Party, I take great pleasure in supporting this bill at third reading. I want to make very sure that the minister understands that her help ensures the integrity of this act which prevents in any way a
bargaining tool based on a monetary support problem, a pension rights problem or a child access or child custody case because it is much more important that the best interests of the child be served. The minister and her parliamentary secretary may well remember how hard we tried to look at the mandatory conditions for access to and support for children who are the main concerns in a divorce issue of this kind.
I appreciate that we have now a tool whereby no one would be able to to use the get in order to obtain concessions in a civil divorce proceeding in this land.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief because certainly we in the New Democratic Party have strongly supported this legislation and, indeed, have urged the government to move expeditiously for its passage.
I just wanted to join on this important occasion of third reading of the bill in commending all of those groups across this land who have worked so very hard with such tremendous dedication and energy to right an historical wrong. I am not going to name all of the groups because inevitably some would be left out, but I do want to take this opportunity to pay tribute particularly to those women who have been responsible for pushing to the point where now this bill will be a reality.
Too many women have in particular suffered the pain and injustice of the current provisions in this area. I would hope that this legislation could serve as a model to provinces which have not yet moved in this important area. I know that some have, but there are others which have not yet taken this step. I would hope that they would move forward in this important area.
Finally, I want to urge the government to proclaim this legislation in the very near future. I had some concern because in questioning government representatives it was suggested that there would be a series of prolonged consultations with provincial jurisdictions. I hope the minister in responding to this might make it very clear that she intends to proclaim this legislation in the very near future.
Injustice has been done and every day that this legislation is delayed, further injustice will continue to be done. I commend those involved.
May 4, 1990

On behalf of the New Democratic Party, we welcome this legislation and we urge the minister to proclaim it as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the member for Mount Royal who has been intimately involved with this bill and all of its stages, has spoken for the Liberal Party for the Opposition.
I am very happy to have the opportunity to come to the House from the Meech Lake committee which has adjourned for lunch and put on the record my own satisfaction about the achievement of this very important piece of legislation.
It was the present Minister of Transport who finally decided for the government that this was a worthwhile measure, a measure which advances Canada's sympathetic understanding of the pluralistic nature of our society, showing a willingness to accommodate, within the laws of Canada, the legitimate interests of multicultural groups.
I hope that this law will not only be of value, as I know it will, to the community concerned, but that it will be the model for ways in which Parliament can respond across Canadian society to various groups when it is possible to do so; to assist them not in the establishment, as there is in some countries, of systems of laws that apply to minorities that live separately within the country but to the kind of pluralistic, proud and integrated society which we are in which this type of legislation permits the accommodation of the particular interests of one minority group.
I have had the pleasure and honour of being supported in all of this, as have other members, by a great many individuals and organizations across the country who have been committed to this cause and who have seen it come forward.
I think it is important to pay tribute on a particular historic day, for the reason I will mention in a moment, to the Attorney General of the province of Ontario, Ian Scott, whose legislature was the first to provide a legislative framework for recognizing the situation of the get, the problem of the traditional Jewish divorce against the Canadian laws and provincial laws that relate to divorce, family law, and child custody. That was the first province to accommodate this problem. As it happens, the Attorney General is in Ottawa today, along with the

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise on the occasion of third reading of Bill C-61, an Act to amend the Divorce Act (barriers to religious remarriage), which I have the honour of tabling.
I would like to echo the comments that have been made about the fine work of my predecessor, the now Minister of Transport. I did have the pleasure of sitting on the cabinet committee to which this proposal came and was interested at that time to see the extent of the consultations which had taken place on the bill and more importantly, the extent of consensus, not only among Jewish leaders in Canada but among all religious leaders in Canada. This was a very important measure to bring forward.
I would like to say a few words for the record about the nature of the bill. The amendment to the Divorce Act, which is inherent in Bill C-61, would provide a court with discretionary power to preclude a spouse from obtaining relief or proceeding under the Divorce Act: first, where that spouse refuses to remove a barrier to religious remarriage; and second, where the power to remove the barrier to religious remarriage is within the control of that person.
The purpose of this bill is to assist Jewish citizens whose spouses are withholding a religious divorce, which is called a get, in order to obtain concessions in a civil divorce. The government did consult every other known religious group in Canada and satisfied itself that they would not be affected by this amendment.

May 4, 1990

During the past 15 years, the divorce rate in the Jewish community has reached the same level as in the rest of the population. Cases of abusing the get have increased at the same rate.
In 1987, the B'Nai Brith Association in Canada did a study of 311 cases that occurred during the four previous years.
According to the study, Jewish women were twice as likely to suffer negative repercussions, and those repercussions were worse than those to which men were exposed in the same situation.

A 1987 study conducted by B'nai B'rith Canada documented 311 cases within the previous four-year period. In the same study, as I said in French, women were found to be twice as likely to be the victims of discrimination and when victimized, they faced greater adverse consequences than men.
The consequences to women deprived of a get and loyal to their faith are severe. They may not remarry within their faith, even though civilly divorced. If they do remarry, children from a second civil marriage are considered illegitimate and restricted from practising their religion. Such consequences to a religious person leave them open to blackmail from the spouse withholding the get. For example, the spouse could say, "Give up your claim for support or custody of the children and I will offer the get." Even those not contemplating a second marriage find it uncomfortable to be considered married within their religion to someone they have divorced civilly.
The vast majority of adherents to the Jewish faith condemn as unfair this practice of bargaining with the get. Yet they are powerless to amend the situation. Persuasion by rabbis has often proved ineffective. Since the dispersion of the Jews there is no central Jewish authority to amend the Jewish legal code, the Halachah-ic, which governs the get. Nor is there any modern-day authority within rabbinical courts to enforce the offer and receipt of gets. Full support for Bill C-61 was expressed by major Jewish organizations who attended the hearings before the legislative committee. Representatives of the three Parties praised the bill and quickly passed two minor technical amendments.
The first amendment dealt with an inconsistency between the English and French versions.
The second amendment removed the word "exclusive" from the term "religious barriers within the exclusive control" of a person in order to more accurately reflect that the get procedure requires the co-operation of a three or five man rabbinical court.
Presidents of both major Jewish organizations, B'Nai Brith Canada and the Canadian Jewish Congress, spoke on behalf of the bill.
As well, the Toronto Board of Orthodox Rabbis and the Coalition of Women on the get endorsed the legislation and the two amendments.
All four organizations view Bill C-61 as an example of the government's commitment to multiculturalism.

Bill C-61 will enable Canada's Jewish community to preserve its traditions without destabilizing models of family life. It also ensures that the principles of the Divorce Act with respect to alimony and custody are applied equally to all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to express appreciation to the other parties for their support and their desire to see the bill passed expeditiously. I believe there will be no delays to the proclamation of this bill.
This bill represents the finest traditions of Parliament in dealing with a sensitive situation in the very, very best interest of all Canadians. Since it is a Friday, I would like to say to all of those who will gain from the bill, Shabbot Shalom.
Mazel Tov, Madam Minister.
